sections.html:
• Name: Spider crab (also the red mangrove crab)
  • Scientific name: Neosarmatium meinerti
  • Minimum tank size: about 40 litres
  • Type: Semi-terrestrial
  • Breeding: Very difficult
  • Size (carapace): 2.5–5 cm
  • Leg span: 7–10 cm
  • Setup: Terrarium or paludarium
  • Moisture: 60% and higher
  • Diet: Mostly herbivore/omnivore
  • Temperament: Semi-aggressive
  • Colour forms: Red-orange and yellow

Neosarmatium meinerti is one of the rarest crab species in the hobby, and little is known about it. It is semi-terrestrial and mostly herbivorous, and can make a great pet in terrarium and paludarium setups.

It is not an aquatic crab. It is also quite destructive and may redecorate the paludarium to its liking, and it is not safe to keep with plants.

Spider crabs are widely spread over the Indo-West Pacific region (Madagascar, Seychelles, Mauritius, Kenya, Mozambique, Somalia, Australia, Sri Lanka, Taiwan, Thailand, Indonesia, Sulawesi, Fiji, Guam, Solomon Islands and New Caledonia).

They are the most abundant and widespread crab species of East African mangroves.

This species commonly occupies the dry and muddy area of the upper intertidal zone associated with mangroves and estuaries, where it digs deep burrows under the canopy and forages on sediment detritus and leaves.

Burrows can reach 1–2 m below the soil surface, ending in a chamber at the level of the water table. They contain only one opening. Most are simple and linear, though some have bends, chambers and side branches. Juveniles (about 1 cm carapace length) do not dig their own burrows but shelter in adult burrows during early life.

In the wild, humidity ranges from 50% to almost 100%, and burrow temperature can be 15°C while above ground it can reach 36°C.

The minimum recommended tank size for one spider crab is about 40 litres, as these crabs need a lot of surface area to roam. As adults, one male and one female may be kept together in an enclosure of 120 litres or more, but two adult males would need far more space to reduce territorial fighting.

The land area should take at least 90% of the space in the tank, or even more.

Spider crabs are very good escape artists, so cover the tank as much as possible.

This species is hardy and forgiving for beginners, but needs a specific setup.

Substrate

Fill the tank with a combination of moist sand or mud in which they can burrow. To dig and form a cave, the substrate must be moist enough to hold its shape when squeezed, but not so wet that it drips or pools water. A mixture of coco fibre and sand gives a "sandcastle consistency". To test it, push a pencil all the way down and pull it out: if the tunnel does not collapse, the substrate is good enough.

Spray the substrate regularly with dechlorinated fresh water to keep it moist. Never use saltwater to maintain moisture, as salt does not evaporate and builds up to harmful levels.

The deeper the better: in the wild they burrow up to 2 m, so at least 10 cm is recommended. Options include Zoo Med Hermit Crab Sand, Zoo Med Eco Earth loose coconut fibre and Carib Sea sand.

Decorations and hiding places

Spider crabs appreciate leaves, rocks, wood, plants, PVC pipes and other decorations. Plenty of hiding places minimise stress and are also critical for moulting.

Care and handling

  • They are not pets to play with; do not take them out without need.
  • Never lift them by the legs or claws.
  • Do not leave uneaten food for too long, as it causes smell and bacteria. These crabs store food in their burrows.
  • Provide as many hiding places as possible.
  • Base the substrate on sand and coco fibre.
  • Keep the lid tightly closed.

Calcium and moulting

To grow and regrow lost limbs, spider crabs must moult regularly. A new exoskeleton needs a lot of calcium. Calcium is found in kale, broccoli, spinach, cuttlebone, eggshells, figs, oyster shells, seaweed, seeds and insects. Always keep a small piece of cuttlebone in the enclosure and regularly feed specialised invertebrate foods. Moulting leaves crabs vulnerable, so many hiding places are essential.

Temperature

The optimal range is 23–28°C, but these are very hardy animals that tolerate a huge range of temperatures. If you use a heat pad, it should cover 1/3 of the tank or less so the crabs can move between warmer and cooler places.

Humidity

Spider crabs are resilient to humidity fluctuations, but 60–80% is recommended for optimal conditions.

Water bowls

Spider crabs do not need much water, so water bowls can be used instead of a complex aquatic setup. The bowls must be deep enough to submerge the crabs completely. Provide one bowl of freshwater and one of saltwater.

For saltwater, use a marine salt such as Instant Ocean, about 120 ml per 4 litres of water. Never use ordinary aquarium salt or table salt.

For freshwater, bottled spring or distilled water is ideal. Tap water must be left to stand for 24 hours first, as chlorine is toxic to them. A water conditioner such as Seachem Prime can also be used.

Lighting has no special requirements; you may not even need one. A digital thermometer and humidity gauge (for example Zoo Med digital thermometer/humidity gauge) are useful for monitoring conditions.

It was initially believed that this species was completely herbivorous, but recent studies show Neosarmatium meinerti is an opportunistic omnivore with a primarily vegetarian diet. Stomach content analysis showed a diet mainly of mangrove leaves with little animal matter. Laboratory experiments showed a crab can consume around 2% of its body weight per day, and leaf consumption per gram of crab was higher in females than in males.

In captivity, they need a good mix of meat and vegetation for best growth. They are avid leaf and propagule eaters, and protein should be at most about 10–15% of the diet.

Suitable foods

  • Vegetables (broccoli, cabbage, carrots, cucumber, lettuce, corn, spinach, peas, squash, leafy greens)
  • Fruits (sweet apple, banana, pear, melon, mango)
  • Leaves
  • Shrimp pellets and granules
  • Fish food (e.g. TetraMin flakes)
  • Shrimp food (e.g. Hikari crustacean food, algae wafers)
  • Frozen bloodworms
  • Detritus worms
  • Brine shrimp

Leaves (Indian almond leaves, dead beech or oak leaves) should always be on the menu, as the crabs feed on them and need their detritus.

Food can be left for 24 hours before removal; leaves can stay in the tank for weeks. Remove whatever is not eaten in a day to prevent mould. Do not give the same food for weeks; change the menu at least weekly. Feeding frequency is daily.

They are not safe with plants: although they prefer old or decaying leaf litter, when hungry they will eat, cut and uproot anything.

Neosarmatium meinerti is semi-terrestrial. It constructs deep burrows to maintain an optimal moisture level and to have a constantly available water source. Although mostly nocturnal, it can be very active during the day.

Spider crabs are quite destructive and may redecorate the paludarium.

Their social behaviour is complex: they are solitary and territorial, yet their burrows are often found close together. Their aggression is lower than in many other popular ornamental crabs.

  • Social: No
  • Active: Yes
  • Peaceful: No
  • Burrowers: Yes

Tankmates

  • They are not peaceful, and it can be risky to house multiple animals together.
  • They are territorial, especially males, which are very likely to fight.
  • Do not let them go hungry: this raises aggression and the risk of cannibalism.
  • Do not keep them with hermit crabs; their digging endangers any hermit crab moulting underground.

Ideally keep a spider crab alone or with crabs of the other sex, well fed and with many hiding places, although even this does not guarantee peaceful coexistence. In a paludarium, dwarf shrimp, snails and fish can be kept with them, as they usually show little interest in entering the water.

• Size: females are generally smaller than males.
  • Abdomen: males have a narrow, slim, triangular plate, while females have a broad plate on the belly.

Breeding in captivity is very difficult. Males and females reach sexual maturity at an estimated carapace length of 17.3 mm and 15.6 mm respectively, although maturity can vary considerably with geographical location; low temperatures slow growth and increase the time needed to mature.

Females release larvae into saltwater in synchrony with spring tides. After hatching, larvae spend an estimated 4 weeks in the plankton. In the open ocean they pass through a number of stages; the last, the megalopa, returns to the mangroves guided by chemical and physical cues.

In nature the species has a distinct spawning peak every year in February, followed by offshore larval development from February to March, so megalopae and first crab stages return to the mangroves in March and April. They then live in adult burrows, in diverticula branching from the main burrow.

Fully grown spider crabs can reach up to about 7–8 cm in carapace length with a leg span of about 12–15 cm, but the average adult carapace width is usually 2.5–5 cm, with a leg span of 7–10 cm.

There are two colour morphs: the dominant red-orange form, with red-orange claws, coloration extending over two-thirds of the proximal outer margin of the palm and fingers fading to yellow; and the yellow form, with yellow claws and carapace. The yellow form is found only in Australia, Taiwan, Guam and the Solomon Islands, and there is speculation about two genetically differentiated groups.

According to a study the species lives about 5 years, and with appropriate care it can probably live longer.

Caring for these crabs is very easy and can be recommended even for beginners; the only problem is that the species is very rare in the trade.
